query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition of Nb (approximately 2 at.%) into the eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote segregation of Nb to the lamellar colony boundaries. This will form a thin, ductile interfacial film that facilitates slip transmission across internal boundaries and reduces the formation of dislocation pile-ups, thereby mitigating local stress concentrations and suppressing microcrack nucleation during room-temperature deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness due to dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base eutectic HEA with 2 at.% Nb via conventional melting and homogenization processing.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing (strain rate ~10^(-3) s^(-1)) and standard ambient operating conditions. Homogenization processing must allow for Nb segregation without formation of coarse, brittle Nb-rich secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, Nb-enriched interfacial layer at the lamellar boundaries that modifies the local chemistry and structure, enabling enhanced dislocation transmission and reducing the severity of dislocation pile-ups.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a tendency to segregate to internal boundaries during solidification/homogenization. This segregation lowers the local misfit and barrier strength at the lamellar interfaces, allowing dislocations to cross over more readily. The reduced accumulation of dislocations alleviates local stress concentrations and delays the nucleation of microcracks, while any minor precipitation effects may also contribute to a slight precipitation hardening, thereby retaining or increasing the overall strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature tensile ductility, potentially on the order of a 30–50% improvement in fracture strain relative to the untreated alloy, accompanied by a maintenance or modest increase (approximately 5–10%) in yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with high strength but limited tensile ductility and premature failure due to dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention depends on achieving a well-controlled Nb segregation at the lamellar interfaces without forming coarse, Nb-rich brittle phases. The intervention is anticipated to be effective under room-temperature quasi-static loading; its influence under high strain rates or elevated temperatures remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements are sensitive to processing conditions (e.g., homogenization time/temperature, cooling rate) and the resulting Nb distribution. There is some uncertainty in the balance between the beneficial interfacial modification and any incipient precipitation effects that could lead to potential embrittlement if not properly controlled.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the baseline eutectic HEA and a second with an addition of 2 at.% Nb. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain. Complement mechanical testing with high-resolution electron microscopy and atom probe tomography to assess Nb distribution at lamellar boundaries and to identify the presence or absence of coarse Nb-rich precipitates.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture strain under quasi-static loading at room temperature
Quantitative analysis of dislocation density and pile-up behavior near lamellar interfaces via electron microscopy
Chemical mapping of Nb segregation at interfaces using atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in fracture strain or if the microstructural analysis reveals no effective Nb segregation (or even the presence of deleterious coarse Nb-rich phases), then the hypothesis that Nb addition enhances ductility while retaining/increasing strength is rejected.
